title: Personal protective equipment
blurb: Gloves, masks, eye protection and aprons: what each protects, when to change it, and the safe order for putting PPE on and taking it off.
question: An ultrasonic scale has just finished. Your mask is damp, your visor is splashed and you need to take everything off before taking the instruments to decontamination. In what order do you remove your PPE, and how do you avoid contaminating yourself?

teach.h: Your barrier against splashes and spatter
teach.body: Dental treatment produces splashes of saliva and blood, flying debris and aerosols from handpieces and scalers. Personal protective equipment (PPE) puts a barrier between these and your skin, eyes, nose and mouth, and also protects the patient from you. Your employer must provide suitable PPE free of charge. Your job is to wear it correctly, change it at the right times, take it off safely and report anything damaged. PPE is the last line of defence, so it only works if you use it properly.

teach.h: What each item does and when to change it
head: Item
Protects
Change or replace
rows: Every patient; at once if torn
Every patient; when damp or splashed
Clean between patients; replace if scratched or loose
Every patient or task; if torn or heavily splashed
Wash after use; replace weekly, or sooner if worn or torn
teach.caption: Patients need eye protection too, because spatter and debris can reach their eyes.

steps.label: Mask
steps.sub: Cover nose and mouth; mould the nose clip

steps.label: Eye protection
steps.sub: Glasses with side shields, or a visor

steps.label: Gloves
steps.sub: Most contaminated: peel off inside out

steps.label: Apron
steps.sub: Break the ties; fold the front inwards

steps.label: Eye protection
steps.sub: Hold by the arms or headband

steps.label: Mask
steps.sub: Hold by the loops or ties

teach.caption: Dirtiest item first, and only ever touch the clean parts: the inside, the ties, the arms. HTM 01-05 (2013) lists the mask before eye protection; most current UK training uses the order shown. Gloves always come off first.

teach.body: The outside of your PPE is contaminated, and the gloves are the most contaminated of all. Removing them first stops you spreading contamination from your gloved hands onto your sleeves, face and hair. To remove gloves, pinch one at the cuff and peel it off inside out, then slide a finger under the cuff of the other and peel it off over the first. Never snap gloves off: it sprays droplets. Eye protection and the mask come off last because they're near your face, held only by the arms and loops.

teach.h: Masks and eye protection: getting them right
teach.body: A fluid-resistant surgical mask must cover your nose and mouth, with the nose clip moulded to your nose. If your glasses keep fogging, air is escaping at the top, so the mask fits badly. Never hang a mask under your chin and pull it back up. Eye protection must protect the sides of the eyes as well as the front. Clean, rinse and dry reusable eyewear between patients. For aerosol-generating procedures where an airborne infection is suspected, a fit-tested respirator may be needed, following the practice risk assessment.

rows.label: Glove box stored beside the sink

teach.note: Wrong-size gloves tear easily and restrict movement. Gloves that tear when you put them on are a sign you need a different size.

teach.caption: Blue circle signs mean you must do this. For manual instrument cleaning, wear heavy-duty gloves, eye protection, a fluid-resistant mask and an apron.

teach.text: The doffing order catches people out. Gloves come off FIRST and the mask comes off LAST, with hand hygiene after the apron and again at the very end. Gloves are never washed and reused.

items: Donning: hand hygiene, apron, mask, eye protection, gloves.
Doffing: gloves, apron, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene.
Gloves: single-use, the right size, changed every patient and at once if torn.
Masks: cover nose and mouth; change when damp; never hang under the chin.
Eye protection: side protection; replace if scratched, cracked or loose; patients need it too.

summary: You can now choose the right PPE for chairside and decontamination tasks, know when each item must be changed, put PPE on in the right order and take it off without contaminating yourself.

A.q: An extraction with a high splash risk is about to start. After hand hygiene, in what order should you put on your PPE?
A.why: Apron first, then mask, then eye protection, and gloves last so they stay clean for the patient.

whyNot.0: Gloves go on last; putting them on first contaminates them as you handle the other items.
whyNot.1: Gloves before the apron and eyewear would be touched by everything else you put on.
whyNot.3: Eye protection goes on after the mask, and gloves are always last.

A.q: Halfway through a long ultrasonic scale, your mask becomes damp. What should you do?
options: Replace it as soon as it is safe
Keep it on until the patient leaves
Pull it under your chin to dry
Wipe the outside with a tissue
A.why: A damp mask no longer resists fluids well, so it should be replaced as soon as it is safe to pause.

whyNot.1: A damp mask lets micro-organisms through, so waiting puts you at risk.
whyNot.2: Hanging a mask under your chin contaminates it and your face.
whyNot.3: Wiping doesn't restore fluid resistance and contaminates the tissue and your hand.

A.q: Why are examination gloves changed between patients rather than washed?
A.why: Gloves are single-use: washing can damage them and cannot reliably decontaminate them.

whyNot.0: Slipperiness isn't the main reason; safe decontamination is impossible.
whyNot.1: Soap doesn't dissolve nitrile, but washing can still damage gloves.
whyNot.2: Staining is not the issue; gloves can't be made safe for another patient.

B.q: An aerosol-generating procedure has finished. What is the safest order for removing PPE?
options: Apron, gloves, hand hygiene, mask, eye protection, hand hygiene
Gloves, apron, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene
Eye protection, mask, gloves, hand hygiene, apron, hand hygiene
Gloves, mask, hand hygiene, apron, eye protection, hand hygiene
B.why: Gloves are the most contaminated so come off first, then the apron, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask and hand hygiene again.

whyNot.0: Removing the apron before the gloves lets contaminated gloves brush your uniform.
whyNot.2: Touching your face to remove eyewear and mask while still gloved contaminates you.
whyNot.3: The mask is removed last, after eye protection, and the apron comes off straight after gloves.

B.q: A colleague removes her eye protection by gripping the front of the lenses. What is the risk?
options: The lenses may get scratched on removal
B.why: The front of eye protection is the contaminated surface; it should be removed by the arms or headband.

whyNot.0: Scratching is possible, but the infection risk is self-contamination.
whyNot.1: Gripping the front doesn't strain the arms.
whyNot.2: Fogging is caused by a poorly fitted mask, not by how eyewear is removed.

B.q: You are about to clean instruments by hand at the sink, where splashes are likely. Which PPE is most appropriate?
options: Heavy-duty gloves, eye protection, mask, apron
Examination gloves, a mask and a full-face visor
Heavy-duty gloves and an apron only
Sterile gloves, visor, mask and gown
B.why: Manual cleaning needs heavy-duty gloves against sharp instruments, plus eye protection, a fluid-resistant mask and an apron for splashes.

whyNot.1: Thin examination gloves don't protect well against sharp instruments, and there's no apron.
whyNot.2: Without eye protection and a mask, splashes can reach your eyes, nose and mouth.
whyNot.3: Sterile gloves and a gown are for surgical procedures, not cleaning dirty instruments.

C.q: A visor has scratches that distort your view but is otherwise intact. What should you do?
C.why: Scratched or cracked eye protection should be replaced: it impairs vision and may not protect properly.

whyNot.0: Cleaning can't remove scratches that distort vision.
whyNot.1: Poor vision is unsafe during any procedure.
whyNot.2: Layering eyewear is a workaround; the damaged visor should be replaced.

C.q: A colleague's glasses keep misting up during treatment. What does this most strongly suggest?
C.why: Misting happens when breath escapes from the top of a badly fitted mask; mould the nose clip properly.

whyNot.0: Room temperature isn't the usual cause; escaping breath is.
whyNot.1: Dirty glasses smear, but repeated misting points to air leaking from the mask.
whyNot.3: A visor doesn't fix a mask that lets air escape upwards.

C.q: Which is the correct way to remove examination gloves?
options: Snap them off quickly at the cuff
Peel from the cuff, turning inside out
Pull each fingertip off using bare fingers
Rinse them first, then roll them off
C.why: Peeling from the cuff and turning each glove inside out keeps the contaminated surface away from your skin.

whyNot.0: Snapping gloves off sprays droplets into the air and onto you.
whyNot.2: Touching the outside of a glove with bare fingers contaminates your hand.
whyNot.3: Gloves are never rinsed; they are removed and disposed of.

reteach.title: The outside is always dirty
reteach.question: Imagine your PPE has been sprayed with paint during treatment. How would you take it all off without getting paint on yourself?

blocks.body: If every outer surface of your PPE were covered in wet paint, you'd take off the messiest thing first, your gloves, so your hands stopped spreading paint. Then you'd remove the apron by the ties, folding the painted side inwards. With clean hands, you'd lift your glasses off by the arms and your mask off by the loops, never touching the front. Micro-organisms are the invisible paint.

blocks.text: Masks and eyewear come off last because they're on your face: you want clean hands when you go near your eyes, nose and mouth.

explain.body: Gloves protect hands, masks protect the nose and mouth, eye protection guards the eyes (front and sides), and aprons protect your uniform and skin. Heavy-duty gloves are used for manual cleaning.

test.q: Which item of PPE is mainly intended to protect clothing and exposed skin from splashes?
test.why: A disposable apron protects your uniform and skin from splashes and spatter.

whyNot.0: A visor protects the face and eyes.
whyNot.1: A mask protects the nose and mouth.

explain.body: After hand hygiene: apron, mask, eye protection, then gloves last so they don't get contaminated while you put on everything else.

test.q: Which item of PPE goes on last before treatment begins?
test.why: Gloves go on last so they stay clean until you touch the patient and instruments.

whyNot.2: The mask goes on second, after the apron.
whyNot.3: Eye protection goes on before the gloves.

explain.body: Gloves, apron, hand hygiene, eye protection, mask, hand hygiene. The most contaminated item comes off first and the items on your face come off last.

test.q: Which item of PPE is removed first after treatment?
test.why: Gloves are the most contaminated item, so they come off first to stop contamination spreading.

whyNot.2: Eye protection comes off after the apron and hand hygiene.
whyNot.3: The apron comes off second, after the gloves.

explain.body: Mould the mask's nose clip; change it when damp. Replace scratched or loose eyewear. Choose the right glove size. Store glove boxes dry and away from sink splash zones.

test.q: A box of gloves is stored beside the sink and its packaging is wet. What is the main concern?
options: The gloves will be too tight
The box is hard to reach
Glove sizes may be mixed up
test.why: Splashes from the sink can contaminate the gloves inside, so boxes should be stored dry and away from splash zones.

whyNot.0: Getting wet doesn't change glove size.
whyNot.1: Reach is not the issue; contamination is.
whyNot.2: Storage beside a sink doesn't mix up sizes.
